rationale: This convergent mixed-methods study examines municipal water-supply and demand-reduction regimes across the 22 largest MSAs in the American Southwest through qualitative analysis of policy documents and media-reported political conflicts plus quantitative regression-tree and Random Forest modeling of the Vanderbilt Water Conservation Index (VWCIb). Across both components, two legal/regulatory mechanism families are co-equally central (`multiple`): `fees_tariffs_subsidies` (tiered pricing, billing structures, rate increases, connection fees, lift charges, rebates, and property-tax subsidies, which also feature in ratepayer opposition to costly supply-increase infrastructure) and `enforcement_sanctions` (mandatory water-use requirements, outdoor watering ordinances, fines, enforcement mechanisms, and residential noncompliance), alongside secondary analysis of `review_redress` (tribal, farmer, and environmental litigation) and `institutional_structure_coordination` (interregional/interstate water rights and state-local governance). `fees_tariffs_subsidies` is selected as the single `primary_mechanism_family` because tariff/pricing structures, rate burdens, and rebates span both the demand-reduction and supply-increase conflict analyses as well as the VWCIb index. The central empirical outcome is `administrative_outcome` (city-level adoption of municipal conservation policies/programs measured by VWCIb, as well as institutional/governance conflict, compliance, and policy retention/reversal). Confidence is medium because municipal rules serve as the contested/adopted policy portfolio explained by partisan voting (PVI) and hydrology rather than exogenous household-level treatments.
